newsitem.title: USA: Republicans seen making fewer House gains in South.
newsitem.headline: Republicans seen making fewer House gains in South.

text.p: As the battle for the House of Representatives comes down to the wire, Republicans may gain only a handful of seats in the conservative South to offset expected losses elsewhere, political analysts said.

Republicans are locked in tight races to win 17 open seats in the South, where veteran Democrats are retiring after decades of control and leaving the party of Lincoln with a potential election-year bonanza.
Less than a year ago, when the so-called Republican revolution was still in full swing, party officials boldly predicted that they would sweep the region and tighten their grip on Capitol Hill.
But nowadays, political experts say, Republicans look headed for a net Southern gain of no more than five House seats.

"It doesn't look like we're going to have a whole lot of changes. Republicans may be able to pick up seats in Alabama, Texas and Mississippi. But they also may lose some in North Carolina, and in Texas," said Merle Black, an expert on Southern politics at Emory University in Atlanta.

Republicans currently hold a 235-197 seat majority in the House with two vacancies and one independent who votes with the Democrats. So Democrats need to pick up 19 House seats nationwide to make a bare majority.

The Republican Party's performance in the South could prove critical to the national battle for Congress. This is because some two dozen of the 73 Republican freshmen elected in the 1994 landslide are vulnerable this year.
Republicans would need every new Southern seat they could muster in order to keep their opponents at bay.

House Speaker Newt Gingrich, whose future as congressional leader depends on the outcome, has become increasingly optimistic about the chances for a Republican win, saying he expects the party to add between six and 30 seats overall.
"It depends on turnout. But I've seen movement almost everywhere in the country in the right direction for us," he said on a recent campaign stop.

Republican leaders are staking their bets on an 11th-hour initiative to drum up votes by warning the public not to give President Bill Clinton a "blank check" in his second term by electing a Democratic majority in the House and Senate.
But one of the most effective ploys of the House campaign has been wielded by Democrats who have accused Republican freshmen of "voting in lock-step" with Gingrich and branded them "Newt's lap dog."

The Washington-based Southern Political Report predicts that Republicans will capture seven of the 17 open seats -- Alabama's 3rd and 4th districts; Arkansas' 2nd; Mississippi's 3rd; and Texas' 5th, 12th and 25th.
Other seats in the region that could go to Republicans are Louisiana's 5th and Oklahoma's 3rd, according to other political analysts.
But Republicans also could lose some Southern seats they won in 1994 including North Carolina's 2nd and 4th; and Texas' 9th.

Emory University's Black said one ironic obstacle facing Republicans is a post-redistricting landscape in which the court-mandated disbanding of minority districts has made it harder for party candidates elsewhere.

U.S. Rep. Cynthia McKinney, Georgia's first black woman in Congress, lost her minority 11th district in 1995. But she is still favored to win in Georgia's new 4th district, where blacks make up only 39 percent of the electorate, despite a bitter contest marred by racial invective.
Analysts say Republican freshman Saxby Chambliss also could have some trouble getting re-elected in Georgia's new 10th district, which nowadays also has a large contingent of black voters.
